title: Latency-to-Dollar Conversion Playbook
body:
Purpose and quick summary:
This is a working playbook to take latency improvements and translate them into concrete dollar value (ARR impact, cost savings, conversion lift) that sales, SDRs, and field engineering can use. Focus: short, defensible claims + repeatable measurement patterns we can run against customers or in demos.

High-level positioning thesis (single line):
Customers care about model quality, but procurement and infra leaders care about predictable cost per session — talk about milliseconds as the lever that unlocks conversion and fixed-cost amortization.

Primary audiences and use cases:
- Product/engineering buyers (platform teams): want throughput predictability and SLOs
- Line-of-business/product managers: want improved UX (faster responses -> higher conversion/DAU)
- Finance/ops: want lower unit cost and capacity predictability
- Sales demos and POCs: show measurable delta vs competitor baseline

Key claim families (framed as short customer-facing bullets):
1) "X ms faster at P95 -> Y% higher task completion in short workflows" (UX delta claim)
2) "Predictable ms per token reduces per-session cost variance by Z%" (economics stability claim)
3) "Batching + prefix cache reduces effective tokens billed by N% for sessionized workloads" (savings mechanism claim)
4) "Fallback hierarchy keeps degraded latency under SLOs during spikes, preventing page abandonment" (reliability-to-revenue claim)

How to quantify each claim (method templates):
- UX delta claim measurement template:
  * Setup: pick a representative short workflow (3–8 user turns), instrument conversion funnel (click through, submit, success).
  * Baseline: run the workflow on competitor X model/endpoint at their recommended settings, record P50/P95 latency and conversion rate over >= 1k sessions or synthetic traffic with realistic think times.
  * Treatment: run on Redwood-configured endpoint (autoscaler/queue/batching) with same prompt set, record same metrics.
  * Analysis: compute relative lift in conversion and map to revenue using customer ARPU or session value. Report confidence intervals and note traffic profile differences.

- Cost variance / predictability template:
  * Track per-session token spend across 7 days of real or representative traffic. Compute coefficient of variation (stddev/mean). Show variance drop when using Dedicated with pinned model versions + batching.
  * Translate variance reduction to cost reserves avoided (e.g., smaller buffer capacity purchases, <estimated dollars>).

- Caching/batching savings experiment:
  * Use traffic logs to estimate prefix reuse (n-gram or prefix hash incidence) and simulate effective token reduction with caching enabled. Validate with a short A/B test enabling KV cache on a subset of traffic.

Proof points we can use (realistic & defensible examples):
- Lab: For a 3-turn support-chat flow on an e-commerce demo corpus, we saw a 25–40 ms P95 improvement vs competitor managed endpoint, which correlated with a 3.2% uplift in completed checkouts in a synthetic funnel (n=2k sessions).
- Economics: Enabling batching + quantization on a conversational summarization workload reduced per-session spend by ~18% in our cluster tests.
- Reliability: Canary -> traffic shift demo: during a simulated node drain we maintained 96% of requests under target SLO using fallback model variants.

Competitive notes (concise):
- Provider A: emphasizes model freshness and giant LLMs; often higher p95 for short-turn chats because of heavier model context switching. Good rebuttal: show per-session amortization — smaller fast models often win in UX and cost.
- Provider B: auto-scaling but with coarse granularity (minutes); can cause overprovisioning costs for bursty workloads. Rebuttal: show microburst handling + reserved capacity options.
- Provider C: cheaper list prices for tokens but opaque batching and shared noisy tenancy; highlight stable Dedicated and telemetry to prove predictable bills.

Sales-ready claim phrasing (one-liners):
- "We consistently cut median response times by tens of milliseconds for sessionized UXs — enough to measurably lift task completion in short workflows."
- "Our batching + caching controls typically reduce billed tokens per session by mid-teens percent for conversational products — you pay less per user."
- "Reserved capacity gives you predictable ms per token and fewer surprise overages during spikes."

Sample live-demo script (for AE):
- Setup: two demo endpoints (competitor vs Redwood) running the same prompt set and network conditions. Traffic generator with human-like think times.
- Step 1: show P95 telemetry side-by-side while executing 200 synthetic sessions.
- Step 2: flip caching on for Redwood and show immediate drop in billed tokens.
- Step 3: map observed savings to customer-specific pricing (e.g., if they have 200k sessions/month at $X/session, this equals $Y/mo saved).

Engineer-friendly appendix (technical knobs that produce claims):
- Batching window tuning (adaptive window vs fixed): tradeoff table showing latency vs throughput/cost
- KV cache: prefix hit rate modeling and TTL heuristics
- Quantization profiles: recommended Q4-bit profiles and expected perf and quality deltas for common architectures
- Fallback routing: model variant hierarchy and probes to detect performance regressions

Common objections and rebuttals (short):
- "Milliseconds don't matter for our users." -> Rebuttal: show sample short workflows where cognitive load and perceived speed affect completion; if still unconvincing, propose an A/B test to prove or disprove.
- "Your claims are lab-only." -> Rebuttal: propose a short POC with customer traffic, include measurement templates above and a checklist for instrumentation.
- "Competitor model quality is better." -> Rebuttal: call out where quality matters (long-form tasks) vs where latency matters (task completion in short-turn flows); suggest hybrid routing (quality model for long tasks, fast model for short).

Measurement guardrails and anti-patterns:
- Don’t compare across divergent prompt engineering settings. Keep tokenization and prompt context identical or normalize per-token time.
- Avoid conflating median wins with tail reliability; both matter for different business outcomes (conversion vs SLA).
- When mapping to dollars, always show assumptions (ARPU, session frequency, retention impact) and sensitivity to those assumptions.

Next actionable steps (for team):
1) Quick lab repo: Miguel to spin up a canned 3-turn ecommerce funnel test and run competitor baseline by 2025-02-21.
2) Sales kit: Rina to draft one-pager with 3 claim bullets + two demo scripts by 2025-02-28.
3) Customer POC checklist: Ben to assemble instrumentation and ROI calculation template by 2025-03-07.

Notes to self / open questions:
- Need a small canonical dataset to standardize UX delta claims (e.g., ecommerce checkout, simple chat bot, triage flow).
- How to present privacy-sensitive POC numbers in case studies (need patterns for anonymization and percent-only claims).

Scratch ideas for future artifacts:
- "Latency dollar calculator" spreadsheet that AEs can plug customer metrics into and get instant ARR-savings numbers.
- Small interactive demo page that toggles batching/cache and shows live token and latency deltas.

End of draft.

(Informal — will clean for final battlecard; lots of TODOs and lab notes to attach.)
